questions.title: What exactly do you mean by "1.58 bits" per parameter when weights are ternary?
questions.question_body: The paper calls the model "1.58-bit" because weights are ternary in \{-1,0,+1\}. I think \(\log_2(3)\approx 1.585\) bits per independent symbol, but I'm confused how this maps to practical storage and throughput claims. Are you counting Shannon entropy per parameter, raw encoded bits, or something else? How does storing ternary weights in hardware (which typically uses whole bytes or 2-bit encodings) justify the "1.58 bits" label?

questions.title: How does the absmean scaling (\(\gamma\)) interact with the quantized weights during inference?
questions.question_body: Equation (1) defines \(\widetilde{W} = \mathrm{RoundClip}(W/(\gamma+\epsilon),-1,1)\) with \(\gamma=\frac{1}{nm}\sum_{ij}|W_{ij}|\). After quantization, are the integer ternary weights multiplied back by \(\gamma\) during inference (i.e., effective weight \(\gamma\widetilde{W}\))? If so, does that multiplication reintroduce FP multiplies into the matmul, undermining the claim of "almost no multiplication"? If not, how is the scale applied or absorbed so that only addition remains?

questions.title: What value is used for \(\epsilon\) in \(\gamma+\epsilon\), and how sensitive is training to that choice?
questions.question_body: The quantization formula uses \(\gamma+\epsilon\) to avoid division by zero. What numeric value did you choose for \(\epsilon\) during training and inference, and did you test sensitivity to it? Could a poor choice cause many weights to quantize to 0 or saturate at \{\pm1\} and hurt performance?

questions.title: How are gradients computed through RoundClip during training?
questions.question_body: RoundClip is non-differentiable (round and clip). Did you use a straight-through estimator (STE) or another surrogate gradient? If STE, what variant and were there any stability issues (e.g., exploding gradients, oscillations) when training from scratch with ternary weights?

questions.title: Are the underlying (latent) weights stored in full precision during optimization, or do you keep them quantized in memory?
questions.question_body: When training BitNet b1.58 from scratch, do you maintain a full-precision copy of weights that receives gradient updates and then quantize for the forward pass, or are weights updated directly in the ternary representation? This affects memory usage and optimizer choices — what did you do and why?

questions.title: What optimizer and hyperparameter schedule were used for training these 1.58-bit models?
questions.question_body: Training quantized networks can require different learning rates, weight decay, and warmup. What optimizer (AdamW, LAMB, etc.), learning rate schedule, weight decay, and warmup strategy did you use for BitNet b1.58? Were they the same as the reproduced FP16 LLaMA runs, or tuned separately?

questions.title: Why does BitNet b1.58 only match FP16 baselines starting at 3B parameters and not at smaller sizes?
questions.question_body: The paper says performance parity appears from 3B upwards. Conceptually, what causes smaller models (e.g., 1B or 770M) to degrade when ternarized? Is it capacity, optimization difficulty, or something else? Any empirical ablations to show the failure modes at small scale?

questions.title: How do you measure GPU memory usage in the comparisons (weights only, activations, optimizer state)?
questions.question_body: Table and figures report that BitNet b1.58 uses 3.55x less GPU memory than FP16 LLaMA. Does that figure include only model weights stored on GPU, or does it include activations (KV cache), optimizer states, and temporary workspace? How are embeddings (which you said remain full precision) counted?

questions.title: Can you explain how matrix multiplication becomes "integer additions only" when weights are ternary and activations are 8-bit?
questions.question_body: The claim is that matrix multiplication with ternary weights and INT8 activations uses only integer additions/subtractions (no multiplies). Practically, if \(A\) is INT8 and \(W\in\{-1,0,1\}\), then each output element is sum of terms \(\pm A_i\). Is the implementation exploiting this by sign-selecting and adding accumulators? How is accumulation precision handled (do you use 32-bit accumulators), and what is the arithmetic cost compared to a standard INT8/INT32 GEMM?

questions.title: How is sparsity (weight zeros) exploited in the kernel? Is computation skipped for zeros?
questions.question_body: Since weights can be 0, do your 2-bit or ternary kernels skip addition/subtraction when weight is 0, enabling fewer ops and memory accesses? Or is 0 represented but still iterated over cost-wise? Did you measure the runtime benefit coming from true sparsity skipping vs. just using ternary sign operations?

questions.title: Why were activations scaled per token to \([-Q_b,Q_b]\) instead of per-tensor or per-channel?
questions.question_body: You say activations are scaled to \([-Q_b,Q_b]\) per token to remove zero-point quantization. What motivated per-token scaling rather than the more common per-channel/per-tensor scheme? Does per-token scaling add overhead (compute per token), and how does it affect distributional drift across layers and batch sizes?

questions.title: What is the exact activation quantization formula and value for \(Q_b\)?
questions.question_body: The paper says activations are 8-bit and scaled to \([-Q_b,Q_b]\) per token but doesn't define \(Q_b\). Is \(Q_b=127\) (symmetric int8) or something else? Are activations symmetric signed ints, and how are non-linearities like SwiGLU handled with quantized activations?

questions.title: When you say "no zero-point quantization", do you mean symmetric quantization only?
questions.question_body: The text says removing zero-point quantization via scaling activations to \([-Q_b,Q_b]\). Is this equivalent to using symmetric quantization (zero point = 0) for activations? If so, are there any corners (e.g., ReLU or SwiGLU outputs) where asymmetric ranges would have helped?

questions.title: How were the FP16 LLaMA baselines reproduced — were hyperparameters, tokenization, and data the same?
questions.question_body: You compare BitNet to "our reproduced FP16 LLaMA" pre-trained on RedPajama for 100B tokens. Did you exactly match the original LLaMA architecture/hyperparameters (learning rate, batch size, optimizer) and data preprocessing? Any differences might explain performance gaps — please clarify reproduction fidelity.

questions.title: How did you compute the 71.4x arithmetic energy savings for matrix multiplication on 7nm chips?
questions.question_body: The energy savings number seems very large. Which energy model or assumptions from references [energycost, pokebnn] were used? Does the calculation include memory movement (DRAM/SRAM), accumulation, scaling by \(\gamma\), or only arithmetic ops? Can you show the breakdown and assumptions (e.g., energy per FP16 multiply versus INT8 add)?

questions.title: Does the absmean scaling constant \(\gamma\) need to be stored for each layer, and if so, how much extra memory and compute does it add?
questions.question_body: If quantized weights are actually \(\gamma\widetilde{W}\) for each weight matrix, you must store \(\gamma\) (a scalar per matrix) and multiply outputs or inputs by it. Are these scalings applied at inference time, and are they done in FP16 (reintroducing multiplies)? How many extra scalars are stored and how are they applied efficiently?

questions.title: How do you quantize or handle embeddings if they remain full precision?
questions.question_body: The paper says embeddings remain full precision and that their proportion of memory decreases for larger models. Why not quantize embeddings as well? Did you try ternary or lower-bit embeddings? How much of the memory advantage would be lost if embeddings were kept in FP16?

questions.title: Is the Ladder 2-bit kernel used to represent ternary weights? How do you encode \{-1,0,+1\} in 2 bits?
questions.question_body: You mention integrating a 2-bit kernel from Ladder. What encoding did Ladder use for ternary values (e.g., two-bit codes mapping to -1,0,+1 and one unused code), and how are lookups/operations implemented to enable sign selects and skipping zero values? Any constraints on alignment or packing?

questions.title: What are the numerical accumulator precisions and overflow considerations during INT8-add accumulations?
questions.question_body: When summing many INT8 values (possibly signed), accumulators can overflow if using 16-bit, so INT32 is typical. What accumulator width did you use in the optimized kernel? Does the energy estimate assume INT32 accumulators, and how does that affect the overall energy and memory-access cost?

questions.title: How is the scale per token for activations computed efficiently at inference time?
questions.question_body: Per-token scaling requires computing a scale factor (e.g., max absolute across activations for the token) and then rescaling. For long sequences and large batches, does this compute overhead become significant? How did you implement it efficiently on GPU, and is it included in the latency reported?

questions.title: What regularization (if any) was used to encourage sparsity (i.e., more zeros) in the ternary weights?
questions.question_body: Ternary quantization gives three possible values; some methods encourage zeros via L1 regularization or thresholding. Did you apply any explicit sparsity regularizer or schedule to increase the fraction of zeros, and does the proportion of zeros correlate with faster inference?

questions.title: How was the per-task zero-shot evaluation performed: prompt templates, temperature, and normalization?
questions.question_body: For zero-shot evaluation on ARC, Hellaswag, etc., what prompts, temperature, and logits post-processing were used? You mention averaging accuracy and normalized accuracy for some tasks—what is normalized accuracy here, and how are ties/baseline corrections handled?

questions.title: Can the rounding/clipping cause a biased estimator such that parameter distributions drift from intended ranges?
questions.question_body: Since rounding is to \{-1,0,+1\} after scaling by \(\gamma\), this mapping could introduce a bias in expectation if the scaling is not ideal. Did you observe drift where \(\gamma\) or the full-precision latent weights adapt to compensate and maintain performance? Any diagnostics of post-quantization weight distributions?

questions.title: How does BitNet b1.58 handle layer normalization (RMSNorm) and biases being removed?
questions.question_body: You adopt RMSNorm and remove biases for LLaMA-alike compatibility. Are normalization parameters quantized or full precision? Removing biases can interact with quantization — did you find removing biases necessary for stability, and what motivated that choice?

questions.title: Is there any theoretical justification for "feature filtering" improvement by allowing zero weights vs. binary \{\pm1\}?
questions.question_body: The paper claims that adding 0 enables explicit feature filtering and improves modeling capacity. Can you make a more formal argument or provide experiments showing how ternary weights enable better representational or generalization properties versus strictly bipolar weights?

questions.title: How was the equivalence mapping between BitNet sizes and FP16 sizes derived (e.g., 13B b1.58 ~ 3B FP16)?
questions.question_body: You provide equivalences like "13B BitNet b1.58 is more efficient than 3B FP16 LLM" — what metric or Pareto frontier did you use to derive these equivalences (latency, memory, energy combined)? Was there a single cost function or multiple separate comparisons, and how should one interpret these mappings?

questions.title: For the 2T token experiments, were compute budgets (GPU-hours) and batch sizes matched to the StableLM run?
questions.question_body: You say you trained a model with 2T tokens following StableLM-3B recipe. Did you match the same total compute (e.g., FLOPs, batch size), optimizer settings, and data preprocessing? If not, could differences in training regime explain the reported superior performance?

questions.title: How reproducible are these results — is code and training recipe available?
questions.question_body: Are the training scripts, model checkpoints, and the specialized kernels (e.g., 2-bit Ladder kernel) going to be released? Without kernel implementations or exact hyperparameters, it's hard to reproduce latency/memory and perplexity claims — what's the plan for reproducibility?

questions.title: Won't the per-layer scale factors and final output scaling cause small FP multiplies in other parts of the network?
questions.question_body: Even if the matmul inner loop uses only sign-add operations, combining outputs, applying RMSNorm, SwiGLU, attention weights, and softmax might involve FP operations. Can you quantify what fraction of total FLOPs or energy still involves FP multiplies for a large model, and are these negligible compared to the ternary matmul savings?

questions.title: How would quantized MoE routing and expert weights be implemented for 1.58-bit models?
questions.question_body: You suggest 1-bit MoE could reduce memory and communication overhead. But routing decides which expert to use and may require higher precision logits. How do you quantize routing and gating networks? Would expert parameters be ternary, and how would you handle the many-to-many communication patterns with quantized activations on real hardware?

questions.title: Are there failure cases where BitNet b1.58 produces worse calibration or more toxic/unreliable outputs than FP16 models?
questions.question_body: Quantization can affect calibration and generative behavior. Did you run any human or automated evaluations of generation quality, calibration (probabilities), or safety/robustness checks comparing ternary models to FP16 LLaMA? If so, what were the findings?
